options.a: Eager and excited.
options.b: Hesitant or unwilling.
options.c: Confused or puzzled.
options.d: Quick to respond.

distractorExplanations.a: That is the opposite meaning; the word but signals a contrast with eventually raising her hand, so she started out hesitant.
distractorExplanations.c: Confusion is about not understanding; the contrast with eventually participating points to unwillingness, not puzzlement.
distractorExplanations.d: Eventually shows she took time before acting, so quick to respond contradicts the context clue.

options.a: An index.
options.b: A glossary.
options.c: The table of contents.
options.d: A caption.

distractorExplanations.a: An index lists the pages where a term appears but does not define it; a glossary gives the meaning.
distractorExplanations.c: The table of contents lists chapters and sections in order; it does not define individual bold terms.
distractorExplanations.d: A caption explains a photo or diagram; it is not an alphabetical list of term definitions.

options.a: The freezing is the cause, and the temperature drop is the effect.
options.b: Both events are causes, and the sentence states no effect.
options.c: The temperature drop is the cause, and freezing is the effect.
options.d: The temperature drop and freezing are unrelated events in sequence.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the relationship: because introduces the cause (the temperature drop), and freezing is what resulted.
distractorExplanations.b: The sentence names one cause and one result; the freezing of the puddle is the stated effect.
distractorExplanations.d: Because signals causation, not just time order; the drop in temperature made the puddle freeze.

options.a: A Venn diagram or comparison chart.
options.b: A timeline of events in order.
options.c: A flowchart of cause and effect.
options.d: A story map of setting and plot.

distractorExplanations.b: A timeline shows chronological sequence; the paragraph compares features of two animals rather than events over time.
distractorExplanations.c: A cause-effect flowchart shows how one event leads to another, not similarities and differences between two subjects.
distractorExplanations.d: A story map organizes narrative elements; this is an informational comparison of habitats, diets, and sizes.

options.a: What is the name of the narrator's younger brother?
options.b: On what day of the week does the story begin?
options.c: What clues show that the narrator's attitude changes?
options.d: Where did the narrator say the family moved to?

distractorExplanations.a: This asks for one stated fact that can be recalled directly, not for evidence gathered and explained across the passage.
distractorExplanations.b: A single stated detail like the day is simple recall; it needs no interpretation of textual clues.
distractorExplanations.d: The question asks what the narrator said outright, so it checks recall of a stated fact rather than use of evidence.

options.a: Assume she refers to Lee because Lee is the noun closest to the pronoun.
options.b: Assume she refers to Ana because the sentence subject is the antecedent of every pronoun.
options.c: Skip the sentence because pronouns rarely affect the meaning of a passage.
options.d: Use surrounding context and identify whether the antecedent is clarified elsewhere.

distractorExplanations.a: Proximity does not settle pronoun reference; the reader must check context because either name could be the antecedent.
distractorExplanations.b: Pronouns do not automatically refer to the sentence subject; with two possible antecedents, context has to resolve it.
distractorExplanations.c: Here the pronoun decides who won, so skipping it loses key meaning; unclear reference must be resolved from context.

options.a: A brief statement of the central idea and the most important supporting details.
options.b: A sentence-by-sentence retelling that keeps every example from the paragraph.
options.c: A statement of the reader's opinion about the topic with one supporting detail.
options.d: A list of the paragraph's most interesting facts in the order they appear.

distractorExplanations.b: A retelling with every example is a paraphrase of the whole text, not a summary that condenses to the main points.
distractorExplanations.c: A summary reports the author's ideas objectively; adding the reader's opinion turns it into a response.
distractorExplanations.d: Interesting facts are not necessarily the central idea; a summary is organized around the main idea and key support.

options.a: Turning off the faucet while brushing teeth saves gallons of water.
options.b: Water is a natural resource found in oceans, lakes, and rivers.
options.c: Some people waste water, while others try hard to save it.
options.d: Families can conserve water through several simple daily habits.

distractorExplanations.a: This is one of the supporting examples; a topic sentence states the controlling idea that covers all three ways.
distractorExplanations.b: Too broad and off focus: it describes where water is found instead of introducing ways to conserve it.
distractorExplanations.c: This vague contrast does not preview the paragraph's purpose of explaining several conservation habits.

options.a: Whether every word is spelled correctly and capitalized properly.
options.b: Whether the sentences vary in length to keep the reader engaged.
options.c: Whether every sentence supports the main idea in a logical order.
options.d: Whether the paragraph reaches the required word count for the assignment.

distractorExplanations.a: Spelling and capitalization are editing for conventions, a later step than checking organization during revision.
distractorExplanations.b: Sentence variety is a fluency and style concern, not the first check for logical organization.
distractorExplanations.d: Word count says nothing about whether sentences support the main idea in a logical order.

options.a: Students completed the assignment in a quick manner.
options.b: Students quickly completed and finished the assignment.
options.c: Students completed the assignment quickly.
options.d: In a quick way, students were completing the assignment.

distractorExplanations.a: In a quick manner is a wordy phrase for quickly, so this is the redundant original, not the concise revision.
distractorExplanations.b: Completed and finished mean the same thing, so this revision adds redundancy instead of removing it.
distractorExplanations.d: In a quick way and the progressive were completing add words without adding meaning, so it is less concise.

options.a: At the beginning of a sentence and for common nouns such as city or school.
options.b: For proper nouns and for any word placed after a comma within a sentence.
options.c: For the first word of each line and for every noun that names a person.
options.d: At the beginning of a sentence and for proper nouns such as specific names.

distractorExplanations.a: Common nouns like city or school are lowercase; only proper nouns naming a specific city or school are capitalized.
distractorExplanations.b: A comma does not trigger capitalization; the next word stays lowercase unless it is a proper noun.
distractorExplanations.c: Nouns like teacher or student name people but are common nouns; capitalize only specific names.

options.a: Paraphrase genuinely, cite the source, and use quotation marks for exact wording.
options.b: Paraphrase by changing a few words, and list the source only if quoting directly.
options.c: Use quotation marks for exact wording, and skip citations for paraphrased ideas.
options.d: Cite the source once at the end, and copy sentences without quotation marks.

distractorExplanations.b: Swapping a few words is patchwriting, and paraphrased ideas still need a citation, not only direct quotes.
distractorExplanations.c: Borrowed ideas need credit even when reworded; skipping citations for paraphrases is still plagiarism.
distractorExplanations.d: A citation does not license copied wording; exact language must be shown in quotation marks.

options.a: A grammar worksheet on subject-verb agreement before drafting begins.
options.b: A graphic organizer with the claim, reasons, and supporting details.
options.c: A finished model essay to copy closely with the student's own topic.
options.d: A spelling list of the key words the student will need in the draft.

distractorExplanations.a: Grammar drills address conventions, not the blocker here, which is turning existing ideas into a draft structure.
distractorExplanations.c: Copying a model replaces the student's thinking and organization; a scaffold should help them structure their own ideas.
distractorExplanations.d: Spelling support helps with editing, not with organizing ideas into a claim, reasons, and details to begin drafting.

options.a: Nice work! This paragraph is really good and well written overall.
options.b: Make your writing better by adding more details throughout the piece.
options.c: Add an example after the second sentence to support your claim.
options.d: Fix your grammar errors before you think about the paragraph's ideas.

distractorExplanations.a: Praise alone gives no location or action, so the student does not know what to revise.
distractorExplanations.b: Too vague: it names no specific place or kind of detail, so the student cannot act on it precisely.
distractorExplanations.d: This puts surface editing before content revision and does not point to a specific improvement.

options.a: 3 students.
options.b: 4 students.
options.c: 18 students.
options.d: 30 students.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides 24 by 8 instead of by 6 (24 ÷ 8 = 3); with 6 equal groups, each group has 24 ÷ 6 = 4 students.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracts 6 from 24 instead of dividing; equal groups call for division, 24 divided by 6 equals 4.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds 24 and 6 instead of dividing the 24 students into 6 equal groups of 4 each.

options.a: 13 square feet.
options.b: 20 square feet.
options.c: 26 square feet.
options.d: 40 square feet.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds the length and width (8 + 5); area of a rectangle multiplies length by width, 8 x 5 = 40.
distractorExplanations.b: Halves the product as if finding a triangle's area (1/2 x 8 x 5); a rectangle's area is the full 40.
distractorExplanations.c: This is the perimeter, 2 x (8 + 5) = 26 feet, not the area of 40 square feet.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides only the numerator by 2; equivalent fractions require dividing numerator and denominator by the same factor.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds 2 to both numerator and denominator; adding the same number changes the value, so 8/10 is not equal to 6/8.
distractorExplanations.d: Inverts the simplified fraction 3/4; 4/3 is greater than 1, while 6/8 is less than 1.

options.a: Halfway between 0 and 1/2.
options.b: Exactly at the 1/2 mark.
options.c: Halfway between 1/2 and 1.
options.d: Just past 1 on the line.

distractorExplanations.a: That point is 1/4, not 3/4; it confuses one fourth with three fourths on the number line.
distractorExplanations.b: The 1/2 mark is 0.50; 3/4 is 0.75, which lies past 1/2, halfway to 1.
distractorExplanations.d: 3/4 is less than 1 because the numerator is smaller than the denominator, so it lies before 1.

options.a: 90 degrees.
options.b: 180 degrees.
options.c: 270 degrees.
options.d: 360 degrees.

distractorExplanations.b: 180 degrees is a straight angle, two right angles together; a right angle is half of that, 90 degrees.
distractorExplanations.c: 270 degrees is a three-quarter turn; a right angle is a quarter turn of 90 degrees.
distractorExplanations.d: 360 degrees is a full rotation; a right angle is one quarter of a full turn, 90 degrees.

distractorExplanations.a: Places the decimal one position too far left; $2.00 divided by 5 is $0.40, not four cents.
distractorExplanations.c: Divides 5 by 2 instead of 2.00 by 5; unit cost is total cost divided by the number of pencils.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies $2.00 by 5 instead of dividing; that would be the cost of 25 pencils, not one.

options.a: Give the answer quietly so the student can keep pace with the rest of the class.
options.b: Prompt the student to use the taught strategy and provide only the planned level of support.
options.c: Tell the student to skip the item and return to it after the teacher checks the work.
options.d: Work the problem aloud step by step for the student and have them copy the final answer.

distractorExplanations.a: Supplying the answer replaces the student's thinking during independent practice and builds dependence on the aide.
distractorExplanations.c: Skipping avoids the skill entirely; the aide should prompt the taught strategy so the student can work through it.
distractorExplanations.d: Modeling the whole solution for copying is over-support; independent work calls for a prompt at the planned level.

options.a: Send the loudest student to the office so the rest of the group can refocus.
options.b: Stop the lesson and lecture the group about respect until everyone is quiet.
options.c: Restate the expected behavior calmly and reinforce students who follow it.
options.d: Ignore the noise for the session and report the group to the teacher later.

distractorExplanations.a: Removing a student is an escalated consequence, not a first response; calm redirection and reinforcement come first.
distractorExplanations.b: A long lecture halts instruction and gives attention to the off-task behavior instead of restating the expectation briefly.
distractorExplanations.d: Planned ignoring suits minor attention-seeking, not a whole group off task; waiting lets the disruption grow.

options.a: Ask the student detailed questions to confirm the story first
options.b: Promise to keep the disclosure secret to maintain trust
options.c: Tell the student's parents at pickup that afternoon
options.d: Follow mandated-reporting and school procedures immediately

distractorExplanations.a: Aides must not investigate; detailed questioning can taint later forensic interviews by trained professionals.
distractorExplanations.b: Staff cannot promise secrecy because mandated reporting requires passing the disclosure to the proper authorities.
distractorExplanations.c: Parents may be involved in the abuse; reports go to authorities and designated school staff, not to family.

parapro-readiness-check-application-004.explanation: The disclosure must be reported through required channels; probing or promising secrecy can cause harm. The wording of the scenario makes this principle controlling rather than the nearby alternatives. Reporting does not require proof, and the paraprofessional should not investigate independently.

options.a: Say 'That's wrong' and give the correct answer so the lesson can move forward.
options.b: Praise the effort without mentioning the error so the student stays motivated.
options.c: Call on another student to give the correct answer for the whole group to hear.
options.d: Identify the specific step that went wrong and prompt the student to try again

distractorExplanations.a: Supplying the answer skips the corrective step; the student does not learn where the error happened or how to fix it.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving the error uncorrected lets the misconception stick; guided practice needs specific corrective feedback.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving to a peer removes the student from the correction and does not show them which step went wrong.

options.a: Explain that goal development belongs to the authorized IEP team and provide relevant observations.
options.b: Draft measurable goals from classroom observations and ask the teacher to sign them later.
options.c: Copy goals from last year's IEP so the student's plan stays consistent this year.
options.d: Write the goals with the parents, since families are members of the IEP team.

distractorExplanations.b: IEP goals are developed by the IEP team at a meeting; an aide drafting them alone oversteps the role.
distractorExplanations.c: Goals must reflect the student's current performance and be set by the team, not copied by an aide.
distractorExplanations.d: Parents are team members, but goals are set by the full IEP team, not by an aide working with the family alone.

options.a: Finish the student's sentence aloud once the intended word becomes clear, to save class time.
options.b: Allow adequate wait time and attend to the student's message without answering for them.
options.c: Ask the student to point to yes/no cards instead, since the device is too slow.
options.d: Have a peer operate the device for the student so the message comes out faster.

distractorExplanations.a: Finishing the message takes away the student's voice; AAC users need wait time to complete their own response.
distractorExplanations.c: Swapping to yes/no cards restricts the student's communication; the device is their access to full expression.
distractorExplanations.d: A peer operating the device replaces the student's own message, which defeats the purpose of the AAC system.

options.a: Let the student help struggling peers by giving them answers to the remaining questions.
options.b: Direct the student to an approved extension task or established early-finisher routine.
options.c: Give the student free time on a tablet game as a reward for finishing first.
options.d: Move the student to the hallway until the rest of the class has finished.

distractorExplanations.a: Giving peers answers undermines their learning; early finishers need a planned task, not an answer-sharing role.
distractorExplanations.c: Rewarding speed with games encourages rushing; a planned extension keeps the student learning without disruption.
distractorExplanations.d: Removal is unsupervised and punitive, and it costs learning time; an established early-finisher routine is the planned support.
